searchText: Hey, <@!211091239112671234> and <@!683653554631868440>, I heard you were discussing JUMPDEST analysis issues. evmone/Baseline is using different bitmap than geth. I only keep 1 bits for valid JUMPDEST locations. I spent some time on optimizing it recently. There is some progress, but not 100% sure of results because on my laptop there seems to be a regression with one of the compilers. Here are the results: https://github.com/ethereum/evmone/pull/306 There is also a more fancy implementation, I will benchmark it some other time. ```cpp for (size_t i = 0; i < code_size; ++i) { const auto op = code[i]; const auto data_len = op - size_t{OP_PUSH1 - 1}; if (data_len <= 32) i += data_len; else if (INTX_UNLIKELY(op == OP_JUMPDEST)) m[i] = true; } ``` Do you have information how fast is the geth analysis? For me the lower bound seems to be ~700MB/s. Finally, I tried to accelerate it with SIMD without success. I can share some code, but I'm SIMD noob. Maybe some SIMD hacker can solve this. There is generic problem description for that: https://notes.ethereum.org/@chfast/fast-evm-bytecode-analysis. I don't but I can look it up sometime. The reason we were discussing it, is that I talked about the old attack with a large initicode, and I discouraged <@!683653554631868440> from using a "append to vector" approach. He thought that you did something like that -- but seems you're using a bitmap, which I was almost certain you would have. The evmone/Advanced uses something heavier, but I'm considering it only for benchmarks right now. I'm currently looking to use the exisiting bitvector approach for saying whether there is a jumpdest. I'll still need more information at the start of each block but can generate that lazily. Problem is saving that information so I can get it fast enough - it will need to be fetched for every jumpdest. evmone/Advanced compresses this information to 8 bytes. <@!425274498732916736> I'll go looking later, but how do you store and retrieve it? In evmone's internal program representation every instruction has additional argument of size 8. It can contain e.g. push data or other things, depending on the instruction. For block gas counting I attach the "block info" to `JUMPDEST` instructions, or insert internal `BEGINBLOCK` instruction in case a block does not start with a `JUMPDEST`. https://github.com/ethereum/evmone/blob/master/lib/evmone/analysis.hpp#L20-L42 Thanks. Right now I have parallel array of pointers, one per instruction. Those that begin a block point to a larger struct with stack and gas info. Your approach sounds more generally useful, and at least tells me I can afford to use that much space.
